course_description:
This course introduces students to web design, user experience (UX), web-based user interface design (UI), and front-end development (FED). Students learn to design and develop human-centred websites through integrated study of design principles, accessibility, ethical practice, and modern development techniques. The course emphasises continuous practice, critical judgement, responsible tool use (including AI tools), and practice-based research to support professional capability in contemporary web design and development.

This course treats web design and development as a practiced capability, not a body of knowledge, developed through structured, continuous engagement that builds both technical competence and professional resilience: capability development through continuous, scaffolded practice.

This course provides a practice-led introduction to User Experience (UX), User Interface (UI), and Front-End Development (FED). You learn by designing, building, testing, and refining real websites across the semester using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

A central feature of the course is ongoing practice and iterative learning. Rather than memorising tools or rules, you develop capability through a structured learning loop: analysing client briefs and user data, translating insights into design decisions, implementing those decisions in code, testing your work, and refining it. This repeated cycle builds technical skill alongside professional judgement.

Applied classes play an essential role in this process. They are assessment-aligned and designed to guide you through key stages of each task. In these sessions, you practise problem-solving, receive feedback, clarify expectations, and progressively develop your work. Assessment is therefore integrated into learning and supports growth over time, rather than evaluating a single final product.

The course emphasises responsive, accessible, and ethically responsible design. You apply UX/UI principles, accessibility standards, and culturally respectful practices in both design and implementation.

You also develop responsible AI decision-making capability. You may choose to use AI tools, limit their use, or deliberately not use them. What is assessed is your judgement - how you verify outputs, maintain authorship, and demonstrate critical and ethical reasoning in an AI-present environment.

By the end of the course, you will be able to design and implement accessible, human-centred websites, use professional development workflows, and clearly justify your design and technical decisions using evidence and structured reasoning.

As a Master’s-level (AQF-9) course, this subject includes a research component. Students use user research, design theory, accessibility standards, and ethical frameworks to inform their decisions, and clearly justify their reasoning through annotated artefacts and reflection.

AI tools may be used to support learning and task completion in this course, and the course provides guidance on appropriate use. Students are expected to apply judgement when using these tools, to check outputs carefully, and to ensure that all submitted work reflects their own understanding. Students are responsible for ensuring that any use of AI complies with academic integrity requirements and is appropriately acknowledged.

learning_outcomes.description: Web Design (including accessibility): Analyse client goals and user research to design human-centred website structures and interfaces, and justify design decisions using UX/UI theory, accessibility standards, and ethical considerations. [THIS LEARNING OBJECTIVE CONTRIBUTES TO AQF9 RESEARCH FOR MASTERS PROGRAMS]

Web Development (HTML, CSS, JavaScript): Develop, implement, and evaluate responsive, accessible web pages using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, following contemporary front-end development practices and coding standards.

Tools for Design and Development: Employ industry-standard tools, including design software, development environments, version control, and verification tools, to support, improve, and document design and development processes.

Ethics in Web Design and Development: Identify, evaluate, and apply ethical principles to design and development decisions, demonstrating awareness of cultural, social, accessibility, and data-related impacts in professional web practice.

Justify the responsible selection, use, adaptation, or rejection of information sources, digital tools, and AI-supported systems within web design and development workflows, demonstrating verification, human judgement, authorship, and academic or professional integrity.

assessment_details.title: Research and Proposal
assessment_details.task_description: Use of AI tools is PERMITTED in this assessment task. This course explicitly develops students’ capability for responsible AI decision-making as part of professional web design and development practice. Students may choose to use AI tools, to limit or constrain their use, or to deliberately not use AI tools, provided that this decision is made thoughtfully, transparently, and in alignment with the course Responsible AI Decision-Making Capability Framework . Where AI tools are used, students are expected to: maintain human judgement, authorship, and decision-making authority, critically evaluate and verify AI-generated outputs, use AI tools to support learning and professional reasoning rather than replace them, and transparently acknowledge and reflect on their use as required by the assessment task. Responsible AI decision-making (including justified use, selective use, or deliberate non-use) forms part of the assessment expectations. What is this task? For this task, you will investigate a design problem, analyse research findings, and develop a clear proposal for the website you will build in the next task. In this task, you will respond to a client brief, using research to inform design requirements and proposing a website that meets the client’s goals, values, and constraints. In your submission: research activities and findings are documented, insights are synthesised into design requirements and principles, and a structured design proposal is presented and justified. If you are unable to attend a class, it is essential that you engage with the activities independently, as they form a core part of the learning required to complete this assessment successfully. More information about the requirements for this assessment item are provided in an Assessment Task Sheet that will be available in the course Blackboard site. assessment_details.title: Website Development
assessment_details.task_description: Use of AI tools is PERMITTED in this assessment task. This course explicitly develops students’ capability for responsible AI decision-making as part of professional web design and development practice. Students may choose to use AI tools, to limit or constrain their use, or to deliberately not use AI tools, provided that this decision is made thoughtfully, transparently, and in alignment with the course Responsible AI Decision-Making Capability Framework . Where AI tools are used, students are expected to: maintain human judgement, authorship, and decision-making authority, critically evaluate and verify AI-generated outputs, use AI tools to support learning and professional reasoning rather than replace them, and transparently acknowledge and reflect on their use as required by the assessment task. Responsible AI decision-making (including justified use, selective use, or deliberate non-use) forms part of the assessment expectations. What is this task? Website Development is your opportunity to turn your previous decisions into a working website. You will implement the website structure, visual and interaction design, and key functionality using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript , while integrating accessibility and ethical considerations in practice. This task recognises that implementation reveals constraints. You may need to adapt parts of your proposal, but you must justify any variations and show how your final build still aligns with your earlier reasoning. What do I need to produce? You will produce and submit a 5-page website deployed online (and committed to version control), implemented with component-based CSS and modular JavaScript. More information about the requirements for this assessment item are provided in an Assessment Task Sheet that will be available in the course Blackboard site. learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 1 To Week 13
learning_activities.topic: Lectures | Weeks 1 to 13 Lectures in this course provide the conceptual foundations and theoretical frameworks for key topics in User Experience Design (UX), User Interface Design (UI), and Frontend Development (FED). Rather than functioning as extended presentations, lectures are designed as guided learning sessions that build understanding through preparation, discussion, and application. Short preparatory videos or podcasts are generally provided before each lecture to introduce core concepts, terminology, and examples. These materials allow you to engage with the foundational content in advance, so that scheduled lecture time can be used for discussion, clarification, and short structured activities that deepen understanding. Key features of lectures include: Conceptual foundations: Lectures introduce and contextualise essential theories and principles, including usability, accessibility, ethical design, and interaction design concepts that underpin effective web design and development. Active engagement: Scheduled lecture time is used for discussion, reflection, and small activities that help you interrogate ideas, connect theory to practice, and prepare for applied work. Scaffolded learning: Lecture topics are carefully sequenced to build progressively across the semester, supporting increasing independence and complexity in applied and assessment work. Industry relevance: Concepts and examples are grounded in contemporary professional practice, helping you develop transferable understanding rather than tool-specific knowledge. Lectures provide the direction and framing for learning in the course, while deeper understanding is developed through Applied Classes, independent activities, and assessment tasks. Attendance is encouraged, and all preparatory materials, recordings, and resources are made available for review. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 1 To Week 13
learning_activities.topic: Applied Classes | Weeks 1 to 13 Applied Classes are the practical core of this course. They are structured, hands-on sessions where you apply lecture concepts directly to design and development work, supported by guided activities and feedback from the teaching team. These classes are designed to reflect professional web design and development practice. Rather than following step-by-step instructions to produce a fixed outcome, you will engage in iterative design, coding, testing, debugging, and refinement. The focus is on developing understanding, judgement, and professional habits through practice. Key features of Applied Classes include: Applied learning: Activities are closely aligned with weekly lecture content, enabling you to put theory into practice immediately through design and development tasks. Progressive expectations: Activities are sequenced across the semester to move from guided practice toward greater independence, mirroring the increasing expectations across assessment tasks. Feedback and support: Applied Classes provide opportunities for formative feedback, discussion, and clarification, helping you identify issues early and refine your approach before assessment submission. Assessment alignment" Applied Class activities are intentionally designed to support the completion of assessment tasks. Work completed in these sessions contributes directly to your progress in A1, A2, and A3. Professional practice habits: You are encouraged to explain your decisions, respond to feedback, reflect on challenges, and make responsible choices about tools and workflows, including the use or non-use of AI tools. To benefit fully from Applied Classes, you are expected to come prepared, actively engage with the activities, and use feedback to inform your ongoing work. If you are unable to attend a scheduled class, equivalent activities and resources will be provided, and you are responsible for completing them independently. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
